title: Associational standing
summary: An association can sue for its members when at least one member has standing, the interests are germane to the organization, and the claim and remedy ordinarily permit litigation without each member’s participation.
notes:
Associational standing allows an organization to represent injured members without proving a separate injury to the organization itself. The Hunt test, as explained in UAW v. Brock, asks whether members could sue in their own right, whether the protected interests relate to the association’s purposes, and whether individual participation is required by the claim or relief. In Brock, a union could litigate a common legal interpretation while state authorities retained responsibility for individual benefit determinations.

The third requirement reflects practical and prudential concerns. Brown Group holds that Congress can authorize a union damages action that would otherwise require individual participation. The first requirement implements Article III: a representative association still needs at least one member with standing for the claim. The assigned SFFA note rejects additional operational scrutiny of a genuine voluntary membership organization that identifies and represents members in good faith.

Distinguish an association’s representation of members from injury to the association’s own operations. Havens recognizes an organizational claim where alleged discriminatory conduct made the organization’s housing-referral work more costly. Conflicts among members also require care: National Maritime holds that disagreement alone does not defeat representative standing, while preserving concerns about organizational procedures, intervention, adequate representation, and a union’s duty of fair representation.
